json.system:
You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 1 of 14, about 992 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

paragraphs.text: I've been doing this sentiment survey of the tech workforce. Surprisingly, designers are just the most unhappy on every dimension. We're unclear right now what is expected of a designer. Someone who might be classically trained in a certain way of working is now feeling like, oh my gosh, I need to really change everything. You believe this is the best time in history to be a designer? We're all extremely early in this process. There's just a huge opportunity for designers. Nobody should feel behind right now. I think that if you literally started today, you're gonna have a leg up on pretty much most people. There's just so much opportunity to change the way we work to make great things. If you look at engineering, it's just a completely new job versus a few years ago. I'm curious how that translates to product design.

Engineers have ten or sometimes, like, hundred times the productivity, but our design team hasn't because the design process still takes time. It's still sometimes you have to try a bunch of things and throw them out. It's still very messy and fluid. We had a podcast with the head of Design Cloud Code, Jenny Wen. She talked about the traditional design process: prototype, mock, test, do the research, iterate, and now there's just no time for that. There are certain features for ChatGPT where we really obsess and we really spend a lot of time. We try a hundred things and we throw out ninety-nine; we finally ship one. And other things, we really embrace building in public. We take big swings, and then we learn quickly.

Do you think AI will ever be an extremely good product designer? I think it already is an incredible product designer. Today, my guest is Ian Silber, head of product design at OpenAI. Ian's been in this role for three years now, which is a lifetime in AI time. Prior to OpenAI, he was at Artifact, the news app from the founders of Instagram that I absolutely loved. Before that, he spent eight years at Instagram.

The role of design is in such an interesting place right now, and Ian has such a unique and insightful and fascinating take on the future of product design and what the AI tools that we use every day will look like in the future. I don't know if you've watched me doing this, but I've been doing this sentiment survey of the tech workforce over the past couple of years. I think it's the biggest survey of its kind where, basically, I survey people in tech about how they're feeling about their careers, their work, their roles, especially with the rise of AI this last year.

I'm curious if you're seeing this yourself in the design community. And if you are, what do you think is going on?

First of all, it's an incredible survey, and it's such great information to have as an industry. I think it's something we need to unpack. I see a mix for sure. I think, like, I can speak most to design. I talk to a lot of designers that are very optimistic and very excited. In my world, I see a lot of that, but I can totally understand why people might be feeling very uncertain. Right? Because there's so much discussion about, well, is the role changing? We see that engineers are working totally different.

json.system:
You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 2 of 14, about 991 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you

You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 3 of 14, about 995 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 3 of 14, about 995 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

```
] }
```

You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 3 of 14, about 995 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 4 of 14, about 997 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

json.system:
You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 5 of 14, about 989 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.

And I think that those continue to be important functions. I think this begs the question: do you think AI will ever be an extremely good product designer? You know, it sounds crazy, but engineers never thought they would be able to write code the way it is now.

So just, yeah, thoughts on just how good AI will get. Maybe one way to put it is I think it already is an incredible product designer. It really is actually already great. The cool thing about it, though, is it's accessible to every single person, and it's a tool that anybody can use. I do think it's really... Now that doesn't necessarily mean that it's like the best visual designer or best at information hierarchy or typography or even user experience and interaction design. It's not necessarily like the best at any of those.

It's impossible to predict where things are going. And like I said earlier, how much has changed in three years? Of course, they're gonna continue to get better. But the way we think about it, and I really do believe this, is like, we're building tools to enable people to be more creative, to do more, to build more. And so it is already a great designer, but it's at your fingertips to kind of figure out how to use it and how to get the best out of it.

Truly understanding what people need. You know? I mean, the human feedback loop of watching people use something and understanding that. The, you know, inventing something new, I think, and then, of course, there's just the pure human kind of take. Right? Like, oh, somebody made this. Somebody had a point of view about this.

json.system:
You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 6 of 14, about 953 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

Checked against the OpenAI pricing page on 2026-09-06, gpt-5.6-luna on 2026-09-16, Deepgram nova-3 (pay-as-you-go batch) on 2026-09-17. per_minute for STT models, per 1M tokens for LLMs. supports_temperature: false = the model accepts only its default temperature, llm-call then omits the parameter; absent = sent as usual. Deepgram is billed at the list price even while the starter credit pays for it: a zero price would move the cost of a job and the size of the daily budget on the day the credit ends.

return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 6 of 14, about 953 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

json.system:
You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 7 of 14, about 989 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 7 of 14, about 989 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".

```

  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
```

You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 7 of 14, about 989 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

paragraphs.text: To send invoices, move money around, set up virtual cards for folks on my team. Does your bank have an API, a terminal native CLI, or an AI ready MCP server? I don't think so. And just recently, they launched Command, a conversational interface built directly into Mercury, which acts as your financial operator. I've been using Command to transfer money around, to figure out what categories I've been spending the most money in, analyze my cash flows. Just today, I used it to find out how much I've made from a specific sponsor over the past year. I just ask, 'How much have I made from X over the past year?' Ten seconds later, I have an answer. It is so freaking cool. Visit mercury dot com to learn more and apply online in minutes. Mercury is a fintech company, not an FDIC insured bank; banking services provided through Choice Financial Group and Column NA, members FDIC.

So I asked a bunch of people that know you well what to talk to you about. Joel Lowenstein, who happens to be the head of design at Anthropic, is a good friend of yours, which I love. He said what he imagines the hardest part of your job is balancing the needs of the existing billion monthly active users of ChatGPT with the need to innovate and push and iterate and invent. I'm just curious how you think about that, how you find that balance knowing you have to cater to both sides.

That's a great question, and it's a really fun part of the way we work. I think that we have vastly different audiences, like, really, really different. I've never worked in this kind of quite spread. You know, I spent eight years working at Instagram. We had a billion users or billions of users maybe. I don't actually know what's right now, but it was a lot of people. The product was pretty simple, and it was sort of, you know, a couple ways you could use it. We did think about creators and larger accounts that had special needs, but this is vastly different where you have someone who's using this to help them come up with the recipe to eat tonight or brainstorm their next haircut or something like that.

Then there's somebody who's transforming the way they're doing farming for their, you know, helping to automate their farm in Japan or something, right? It's just like the broadest spectrum ever. Generally, what we've seen is that we believe in this idea of this sort of capability overhang where the product, you know, like, the vast majority of the people are getting a sliver of the true value that they could out of the bottle. That's not necessarily a bad thing; many, you know, they're still getting tons of value.

But we found that we make sure to focus on creating an extremely simple, streamlined experience for many, many people. Then we put all of the cutting-edge stuff. We also make sure to give that and make sure that's really accessible for the people that care. The challenge, of course, is not necessarily over-indexing and sort of putting something that people might not understand in front of a billion users. But generally, what we've seen is we can experiment early with the people that really care, and that's where we have our desktop app, and we have Codex.

Now Chatchify Work is kind of stepping into a much broader audience, which we're really excited about. Eventually, what we want, what we know, and we think about this a lot in design is that things will truly become for billions of users when they don't have to think about a switch or a mode or anything like that. We know that eventually, it has to get distilled into that main experience.

But it is a really fun thing to balance, and we have to think about people that are using this for free every day to people that are paying us hundreds of dollars and lots of different needs. It's just a matter of balancing. As a designer, it does add a lot of complexity for sure to think. You really have to have empathy for every sort of different type of user. But this makes it fun for sure.

That is such a mind-blowing point you're making about the spectrum of usage of ChatGPT and Codex. I didn't think about it that way. Is there has there been a product that has such a wide spectrum from this? Like, what's this rash on my finger to building Salesforce? You know? Yeah. And it makes it really hard to, you know, because a lot of it's so funny. One of the big challenges we're always thinking about is this, like, blank box problem.

People talk about this all the time. It's like, is chat really the final frontier? It's a terminal bay; it's a glorified terminal. It is some critique that I think these chatbots get. Then it's like, okay. So how do you design something that can kind of shape-shift into anything? You know? It's like maybe someone is coming here for image generation for fun or they're trying to generate a PowerPoint. So having this adaptable interface is a really interesting design challenge.

json.system:
You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 9 of 14, about 983 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 9 of 14, about 983 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

json.system:
You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 10 of 14, about 939 words: expect to
return around 9 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as

- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.

paragraphs.text: There's a universal input that you can ask that knows when it needs to answer quickly or should be chatty, or whether it should go off and do work for you. That's a big excitement that we can get to: how can we continue to simplify the experience such that you shouldn't have to think about how this works? You shouldn't have to think about what model you're on or what sort of speed you're using. That goes back to balancing the different kinds of personas and user needs. Of course, we want to expose that for the right people, but we want to ensure that we can get a default experience that works great for most people.

But, yeah, I think it's gonna be really proactive. I do think that we're going to get much richer input through voice and richer visual outputs that are more interactive. I think that you'll start to build more durable workflows with ChatGPT that you can use over and over. Right now, it often feels like you're starting from scratch each time, and we want to make this the tool that you can use to help you with whatever task you have. This all sounds wonderful. I can't wait.

Just zooming out a little bit, I want to talk a little bit to designers again. You're in this epic role right now. I imagine there are a lot of surprises as you entered OpenAI and took on this role. What's something you wish you'd known? What's something you wish you could whisper into Ian of day one to give you some advice? I mean, so many things. The first one is recognizing that we're really early. I was pretty intimidated coming to OpenAI, if I'm being honest.

I remember interviewing and thinking, oh no, I gotta, you know, GPT-4 had kind of recently come out, and I was like, what is all this stuff? Like, I was using it, and I was using the stuff, but I didn't feel like I had a true understanding of it. To be honest, I still have so much to learn. That idea of, like, you are early. We're figuring this out. Like, that, I think I would want to hear.

And the other thing, like, that I found, you know, and for me, this is more personal. It's less about AI or anything, but I stepped into a really different role. Most of my career, I've managed before, but never at a scale that's growing so fast and at a company that is so different. Every day was something new. For a long time, I felt like I was kind of bad at this or I didn't know what I was doing.

And then I went and talked to friends that had led really large design teams or were in a similar transition as me, and they all felt exactly the same. Or the problems that I had were not unique. I guess this is more personal advice: at any stage of your career, there's that feeling of impostor syndrome and wondering what you're doing. I don't know how to do this. Finding people you can talk to who are going through similar things is really helpful.

Finding that community has been helpful. So yeah. So, like, that and then understanding that this is all so new and evolving really quickly. That is extremely helpful to hear. Elena Furnea had this really great post. I don't know if you know her. She's had a growth at Lovable right now.

She had this great post called 'Stop the AI Confidence Theater,' where she just kind of is like, all these people just keep posting all these things they've done with AI and how it changes their lives. It's just not true for most people. Very few of these things are actually that great and working. It's better to be humble about it and say, 'Wow, I don't know. This is changing quickly.' Embracing it and seeing where it goes is important. That connects to what you said about a core component of people doing well right now: those who are curious and just poking around, trying these things again, because maybe it didn't work before, but now it does.

json.system:
You are a transcript editor. You turn a raw speech-to-text transcript into clean, readable text
without changing what was said.

## Input

The user message contains one chunk of a transcript as lines in the form `[start_seconds] text`,
where `start_seconds` is the time the segment begins. Segments are in chronological order. The
speech is in language `en` (ISO 639-1). If a `CONTEXT` section is present, it holds
the last paragraph of the previous chunk; use it only to understand where the text picks up. Never
repeat it in the output.

Video title: `Chatbots are not the final interface: OpenAI’s Head of Design on what’s next | Ian Silber`. Chunk 12 of 14, about 998 words: expect to
return around 10 paragraphs and never fewer than 3. A chunk returned as one
paragraph is rejected: every timestamp inside it is lost.

## What to do

1. Remove filler words, false starts, stutters and immediate repetitions ("э-э", "ну", "значит",
   "um", "you know", "I I think" → "I think").
2. Join fragments that belong to one sentence; the STT splits sentences at random points.
3. Fix obvious recognition errors using context (a term misheard as a similar-sounding word, a
   name spelled three different ways). Keep the correction minimal: change a word only when you
   are confident what was actually said.
4. Add punctuation and capitalization. Write numbers, abbreviations and technical terms the way a
   careful editor of this field would.
5. Split the text into paragraphs. A new paragraph starts when the thought changes: a new topic, a
   new example, a question from the audience, a summary, a change of speaker in a conversation.
   Aim for paragraphs of 3–8 sentences (roughly 40–120 words); a paragraph must not exceed 250 words.
6. Remove non-speech markers that come from subtitles or STT: `[Music]`, `[Applause]`, `[Laughter]`,
   `♪`, sound descriptions in brackets, and the line breaks subtitles insert mid-sentence.
7. Keep lists, code, commands, formulas and numbered steps that the speaker reads aloud as they were
   said, item by item; do not compress them into prose.

## What not to do

- Do not summarize, shorten, reorder or paraphrase. Every sentence the speaker said stays, in the
  speaker's own words. The output is the transcript, not a summary of it.
- Do not polish the style. Conversational phrasing, the speaker's register, their favourite words
  and sentence rhythm stay. You remove noise, not personality.
- Do not translate. The output stays in language `en`, even if quotes or terms in
  other languages appear inside.
- Do not add anything the speaker did not say: no headings, no comments, no bracketed notes.
- Do not merge the `CONTEXT` paragraph into your output.

## Typography

Follow the typography of `en`: for `ru` use «ёлочки» for quotation marks and the
dash «–» with spaces around it; for `en` use straight double quotes "like this" and the dash "–".
Never use programmer quotes "" or the hyphen as a dash in Russian text.

## Output

Return only a JSON object, no markdown fences and no commentary:

```
{ "paragraphs": [
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 1>, "text": "Paragraph 1 text." },
  { "start": <start_seconds of the first segment of paragraph 2>, "text": "Paragraph 2 text." },
  ...
] }
```

- `start` is the `start_seconds` of the first segment that contributed to the paragraph, copied
  exactly from the input. It is checked against the input timestamps: a value that is not one of
  them is rejected, and so is a paragraph longer than about 250 words, since a chunk returned as
  one paragraph loses every timestamp inside it.
- Paragraphs are in chronological order and cover the whole chunk. The first paragraph starts at
  the first segment of the chunk (after `CONTEXT`, if any).
- Text is plain text. No markdown inside strings.

If the chunk is empty or contains no speech (only music markers such as `[Music]`), return
`{ "paragraphs": [] }`.
